archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (offense-led rebuild)
archetype.definition: A 2-6 team whose efficiency sits near league average, a huge jump from last year's bottom-of-the-league side, with a record dragged down by close losses, a leaky pass defense and a sloppy line.

report.headline: A near-average team wearing a 2-6 record, losing close games it competes in
report.take:
The Jets are not a good team yet, but they are not the team the standings describe. Their net EPA of -0.002 ranks 19th. Last season it was -0.271, dead last, in a 3-14 year. They have covered two-thirds of their spreads, seventh in the league, which is the market admitting it keeps underrating them. The point differential of -18 implies about three wins rather than two. Most of the six losses came by a score or less, and a one-score win rate of 0.2 ranks 27th. That is part bad luck and part real failure to close.

The engine is Geno Smith's passing game, and it has accomplished a lot behind a poor line. Pass EPA per play ranks 10th. Meanwhile the line allows a sack rate of 0.087 (28th), a pressure rate that ranks 25th, and a run-stuff rate that ranks 29th, with backs averaging 2.1 yards before contact. The offense has also been heating up. Smith's pass EPA in the last three games was 5.9, 12.2 and 11.7, and the scoring went 19, 25, 33. Garrett Wilson is the clear focal point with 63 targets, and the two tight ends, Kenyon Sadiq and Mason Taylor, soak up much of the rest.

The defense is split down the middle. Against the run it is legitimately good: rush EPA allowed ranks 7th and it misses few tackles. Against the pass it is 25th in EPA allowed and 31st on short throws. Teams don't need to beat this defense deep; they can just work underneath. Over the last two weeks Miami and Las Vegas put up 28 and 38 points, and the offense's improvement has been cancelled out by that slide. Penalties add to the problem at 8.3 a game (26th), including a 156-yard mess against Green Bay.

From here, expect the Jets to keep being competitive and keep losing more often than not. The offense is real enough to stay in games. The pass defense and a now-banged-up front, with David Bailey, Joseph Ossai and T'Vondre Sweat all out, will decide whether some of those close losses start flipping.

strengths.title: Efficient passing despite the protection
strengths.body: Smith's pass offense ranks 10th in EPA per play while the line ranks near the bottom in sack and pressure rates allowed. A 2.92-second time to throw (10th) suggests he is holding the ball to let routes develop and still producing. Doing this well despite the protection, rather than because of it, makes it more likely to last. The recent run of efficient games suggests the offense is settling in.

strengths.title: A run defense that holds up
strengths.body: Rush EPA allowed ranks 7th and the missed-tackle rate ranks 7th, so teams aren't grinding this defense down on the ground. The unit tackles well and lead backs have been held under their averages. Sweat going to injured reserve thins the interior, so this edge may shrink for a few weeks.

strengths.title: Competitive every week
strengths.body: The Jets have covered 66.7% of their spreads, and the differential implies roughly a win more than they have. Under Glenn they also go for it on fourth down more than anyone, which keeps drives and games alive. For a franchise that has been non-competitive for years, the floor has clearly risen.

concerns.title: Short passing defense gets carved up
concerns.body: This is a real flaw, not noise. Pass EPA allowed ranks 25th and EPA allowed on short throws ranks 31st, so offenses can move the chains with easy completions. The pass rush still produces sacks (8th in sack rate), but with Bailey and Ossai out that cover for the secondary weakens. The recent 28- and 38-point games fit this pattern.

concerns.title: Offensive line can't block
concerns.body: The line ranks 28th in sack rate, 29th in stuff rate and 27th in yards before contact. The run game's middling numbers come from the backs and from Smith's scrambles rather than from the blocking. Without a personnel change this lasts all season, and it caps the offense against any defense that can rush.

concerns.title: Can't finish close games
concerns.body: A 0.2 one-score win rate (27th) is partly variance that should regress. Penalties at 8.3 a game (26th) are a self-inflicted share of it. The franchise's recent history shows the same habit, with one-score records below .500 most years. Some of this luck should even out, but the discipline issue is real.

trend.note: The offense has climbed steadily, with three straight efficient passing games and rising scores, peaking at 33 points against Las Vegas. The defense has gone the other way, allowing 28 and 38 in the last two, so the results haven't followed.

nextGame.headline: At Kansas City, an elite team that has won every close game
nextGame.body:
Kansas City is 5-2 with the league's second-best net EPA. It allows 17.2 points a game (2nd) and leads the league in turnover differential per game. There is some luck in the record: KC has won every one-score game and sits a win over expected. Its offense passes well above expectation (3rd) and runs the ball better than anyone by EPA. That attacks the Jets where they are weakest, on short throws, while also testing the run defense. On the other side, KC's pass rush barely exists (31st in sack rate). That is the best possible news for a Jets line that has struggled all year. The Book has KC at -9.5 with a 46.5 total.

Availability cuts both ways. The Jets lose LB David Bailey (81% of snaps), DE Joseph Ossai and DT T'Vondre Sweat, gutting the front that has been their best unit. Breece Hall is expected back, which helps a run game that has relied on Braelon Allen. Kansas City is without both top corners: Mansoor Delane (79% of snaps) is out and L'Jarius Sneed is on injured reserve. That could make KC's strong numbers against opposing WR1s and WR2s look worse on Sunday.

waysToWin.title: Clean pockets, attack thinned corners
waysToWin.body: KC ranks 31st in sack rate and 20th in pressure rate, so Smith should have rare time to throw. With Delane and Sneed out, Wilson gets a weakened secondary. KC is also 21st in EPA allowed on deep passes, so shots downfield are there.

waysToWin.title: Feed the tight ends
waysToWin.body: KC allows tight ends 3.5 PPR points over their averages (29th), and tight ends draw an outsized share of targets against it. With Sadiq and Taylor both involved, the middle of the field is the soft spot.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage
waysToWin.body: KC's special teams cost it 2.19 EPA a game (28th), while the Jets' units are positive. A field-position edge plus the usual fourth-down aggression can steal points in a game the Jets need to keep close.

waysToLose.title: Mahomes picks apart the underneath
waysToLose.body: KC throws more than expected, and the Jets are 31st against short passes. With the front depleted, the pass rush may not save the coverage. KC's line allows the third-lowest sack rate, so a long day of easy completions is the likeliest script.

waysToLose.title: Short-handed front loses the run fight
waysToLose.body: KC has the league's best run EPA. Without Sweat, Bailey and Ossai, the Jets' best unit is missing key bodies. If KC runs at will, the Jets lose the time of possession and the ability to shorten the game.

waysToLose.title: Drives stall in the red zone
waysToLose.body: KC allows touchdowns on just 26.7% of red-zone trips (2nd) and forces turnovers at a high rate. Field goals and a giveaway would turn a competitive game into a cover-only effort.

nextGame.watch: Whether Smith turns the clean pockets against KC's missing corners into points, or just into yardage that stalls in the red zone.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense looks sustainable. It has been efficient against a range of defenses despite poor blocking, and Hall's return adds juice. The one-score losing should ease somewhat, since close games tend toward a coin flip over time. But the short-passing defense and the penalties are structural and will keep costing them. The schedule is lopsided. Buffalo twice, Denver, New England and Minnesota's top defense are hard games. The Chargers, Miami and Arizona are games this team should be favored to win or close to it.

A realistic finish is a mid-single-digit win total with more covers than wins. That would be a clear step from last year and a sign the rebuild is working, even without a playoff push. If the front gets healthy and the close games start breaking even, the high end of the range is in reach.
swingFactors: Health of Bailey, Ossai and Sweat up front
Whether the line can keep Smith upright against Buffalo and Minnesota

confidence.note: Eight games with a stable QB and consistent efficiency, but the close-game luck and new defensive injuries add noise.
